candidates.title: Show HN: I made a technical trivia quiz app graded by AI
candidates.raw_content: Hey HN, I procrastinate looking for a job by creating side projects. This one was born when I finally decided it was time for look for a job. Naturally, I wanted to prepare for an eventual interview and asked Claude to drill me. It did an OK job but the questions were mostly bad and the process was not great. So I decided to build a library of good questions first and still get AI to grade and help me with the answers. And created a web app for it. Among my family and friends, non-technical topics turned out to be more popular so I kept adding those too. The app uses Jev to grade the answers (was using gpt-oss-120b before Jev was released) and different models from OpenRouter to compose the feedback for wrong/incomplete answers. The app itself is pretty simple but the admin is probably the coolest part, including a 4-part AI jury for fact-checking questions and rating them for difficulty and correctness, among other things. Had a lot of fun building this. Anyway, give it a try and let me know what you think! Accounts are optional - only if you want to have streaks and stats and other QoL stuff. Detailed answer feedback will eventually be gated behind a paid subscription but in the Beta it will be available to anyone with an account. candidates.title: I asked Secretary Duffy what Americans should be able to do, if we get this decade right, that they can't do today. Sean Duffy is the Secretary of Transportation, and he sat down with me at our Startup Industrial Base event in DC today. He went straight to how our country's air traffic gets managed. At the command center, people sit in front of six screens with a paper flight chart above them, trying to make the calls on weather and routing. His example: four planes reach the same runway at the same time and only one can land. See it two hours out, speed up two, slow one down, and each one lands when the runway is open. "Like, not complicated stuff, but we don't do any of this." Paper and pencil and minimal human augmentation from software looks like this: Say an airport can take 15 planes in a 15 minute window. "Well, the airlines will schedule 32." He says he's handing the airlines that data and asking them to spread out. The tool is SMART, from Air Space Intelligence, a small company he says competed with the biggest companies and won. It predicts. His stage example: a 2.5 hour ground stop might only need 45 minutes. He's taken heat for supposedly handing air traffic control to AI. Duffy's answer? "it's dumb AI, not smart AI." Controllers still make every call. None of this needs a breakthrough. It needs the will of the people to know they need to use software and be ok with AI augmentation instead of insisting on a paper chart and copper wire.

candidates.title: There's a huge opportunity right now in being the deployment layer for AI into the economy. The amount of work it takes to change out workflows in enterprises tends to be far greater than anyone realizes or would prefer. Clearly this is what the applied layer of AI is going to look like in the form of software and agents, but also it opens up new services firms opportunities. Legacy systems need to be moved to the cloud, data organization and access needs to be updated, software needs to be connected to agents in new ways, workflows need to be reengineered for agents, HITL needs to be figured out for the process, evals need to be generated and maintained, and the entire system needs to be continually updated as new models get released and new capabilities emerge. And the full list may even be longer. AI is not the same as just deploying software. Software you generally did the implementation of an existing, well understood category of technology, then stepped back and the customer kept running. With AI agents, you're delivering actual work augmentation to the organization, which has a completely different set of complexities associated with it. You're no longer deploying tools that the company is merely enabled by, you're deploying work output in a process. Completely different implementation and enablement process. As a result, this is going to open up lots of new kinds of firms and plays for existing firms to diffuse AI into organizations. We're going to see approaches by industry, by size of company, and by problem inside of companies. Traditional SIs will modernize and adapt (some will clearly not adapt as well), and new entrants will also be founded in this period that take advantage of this window. Great time to be an FDE or FDE firm.

It makes building easier but dramatically raises the floor on what it means to be a great startup.

candidates.title: It’s interesting to contrast, what different companies take for granted in their internal cultures I’ve only been at OpenAI for about a week, and the thing that stands out is absurdly high bias towards action This shows up in ways big and small… Sometimes you have a casual discussion about a possible feature, and the PR is sitting in front of you by the time you get back to your desk Or you meet someone on Slack and say: “let’s grab lunch next week” and the meeting invites on your calendar within the next five minutes This has its downsides. because it often feels like everything’s behind a hair trigger, and things just change out from under you— but you can’t really teach this energy, and if you ever lose it, it’s unbelievably hard to get it back Open AI is not a tiny company anymore. It’s got several massive buildings in San Francisco, it’s impressive that this energy still persists
